new_statements.quote: There are no phonemic length or tone in Are. Stress in Are is predictable and occurs on the penultimate syllable. If the stressed syllable is a V or CV, stress is realized through lengthening of the vowel in the stressed syllable. ˈbe.sa 'banana' ˈku.kou 'dog' ni.ˈu.ra 'coconut' to.po.to.ˈpo.na 'name of a fish' [...] When there is a word final closed syllable, it is likely that the stress goes to the ultimate syllable. In this case no lengthening takes place in the penultimate syllable. However, the ultimate closed syllable does not change in length, pitch or strength either. new_statements.rule_in_words: No contrastive stress, length or tone. Word stress falls on the penultimate syllable and is realised mainly as lengthening of the penultimate vowel; a stressed penultimate CVV syllable keeps both vowels (it is exempt from the general CVV->CV vowel-deletion process). Words ending in a closed syllable (the only coda is /m/, historically *mu) probably carry stress on the final syllable instead (a.na.ˈkam), and a closed penult followed by an open final behaves the same way (ka.bi.ˈtam.ni), with no lengthening cue.
new_statements.exceptions: Final closed (/m/-final) syllables likely take the stress (authors hedge: 'it is likely'); penultimate CVV syllables in isolation/pre-pausal position realise stress only by resisting vowel deletion; reduplicated identical vowels merge into one long vowel (apoːˈpopo). Orthographic word division splits inflectional prefixes from the stem, so the phonological word for stress includes prefixes (a.na.ˈkam, to.po.to.ˈpo.na).
new_statements.domain_note: Statement is about the (phonological) word, illustrated with citation forms; CVV behaviour is described relative to pause ('said in isolation or as the last word in a string of speech'). Draft OPD based on 10 months of fieldwork and a 2005 alphabet workshop; villages Mukawa, Bogaboga, Ginada, Irikaba, Wabubu, parts of Dabora.
new_statements.identity_note: The OPD describes Are [mwc] = Glottolog aree1239 as spoken at Mukawa, Bogaboga, Ginada, Irikaba, Wabubu and parts of Dabora on Cape Vogel (the 'Are chain' of Are-Taupota); 'Mukawa' (Giblin 1923, Ray 1907) is the older mission name for the same language. No dialect differentiation is made in the stress statement.

sources.note: pp. 4-5 'Suprasegmentals': no phonemic length or tone; stress predictable on the penultimate syllable, realised as vowel lengthening in V/CV syllables; a stressed penultimate CVV keeps both vowels (exempt from vowel deletion); when the word ends in a closed syllable (always /m/-final) stress 'is likely' on the ultima, with no lengthening.
